name: ORLO-Zig (simulation)
about: ORLO-Zig: the assembly-dynamics simulation. It compares robot counts and build paths for a 10x10 tile structure, and sizes the reaction wheels.

items.title: How the simulation works
items.alt: How the simulation works
items.body:
What it is
A Python simulation of robots building a 10x10 grid of square tiles in free space. Each tile is about 160 mm (0.160 m) on a side, so the finished array is about 1.44 m across. No ground holds the structure. When a robot moves one way, the structure turns the other way, because the total angular momentum stays zero.

How it works
1. params.py holds every physical number (masses, sizes, speed limits). No other file has its own numbers.
2. A path file sets the build order (snake, spiral, backbite and others) and the type of each tile.
3. The rail and motion files turn the path into robot positions and speeds over time, inside friction and turn-speed limits.
4. momentum_core.py tracks every moving body (robots, gantry, tiles) in 6 degrees of freedom. It finds how far the structure turns at each moment.
5. validation.py checks the results against tolerances. A run that fails a check stops with an error.
6. Search and comparison scripts run many build orders and robot counts, and rank them by build time and final tilt.
7. wheel_sizing.py finds the momentum a reaction wheel must store to hold the structure still, and compares flown wheels.

How it was built
I wrote the code with AI coding agents (Pi). Each step had a written task with acceptance criteria and a test for each criterion. More than 30 test files check the physics: momentum conservation, known analytic cases, and checks that must fail when a fault is injected.

Source code: private repository (michaelkuhl10/orlo-zig). Ask me if you want access.

items.title: Next step: a lighter tile and structure (in progress)
items.alt: Next step: a lighter tile and structure (in progress)
items.body:
What changed
The tile is now thicker (30 mm, up from 10 mm). It is mostly ABS plastic, with 8 small servo motors and 4 steel pads. The old structure weight of 65 kg was a guess based on a solid tube. That is too heavy for plastic tiles.

New numbers (first estimate, not checked by a test run)
1. Structure: about 15.5 kg. It is four thin steel posts, ring frames, a base plate and small brackets.
2. Robot dry mass: about 35.5 kg, down from 85 kg. This is the structure plus the 20 kg crawler.
3. System total: about 79 kg, down from 135 kg.

How it was sized
A hand calculation assumes a launch load of 10 g along the stack and 3 g sideways. The post margins are thin (about 1.5 to 2.2). The load case is an assumption, not a real launch vehicle.

What is still open
1. The servo, ABS fill and fastener masses are guesses.
2. The 20 kg crawler has no parts list.
3. The 3 m tall stack on a 0.2 m base has not been checked for tipping or stiffness.
4. The current simulation cannot take a new tile thickness or stack height. It needs a code change before the old analyses can be re-run with these numbers.

Every value in the new sheet carries a status: measured, CAD, datasheet, estimate or guess. Fusion CAD data will replace the guesses.

items.title: Two mirrored robots, no reaction wheels
items.caption: The same build with no wheels at all, seen from the (+x, +y, +z) corner. In step, yaw and pitch cancel, and only roll is left (peak 16 degrees, final 0.4 degrees). If robot B is 0.25 s late, the structure also yaws up to 12 degrees.

items.title: Two mirrored robots, roll and pitch wheels only
items.caption: The same build with ideal wheels on roll and pitch and no yaw wheel, seen from the (+x, +y, +z) corner. In step, the structure stays still. If robot B is 0.25 s late, the structure yaws up to 12 degrees.
items.alt: Two 3D corner-view animations of two robots building each half of a 10x10 tile grid with roll and pitch wheels, with a yaw-angle plot below.
